error_modes.label: Altitude control through all flight phases

texts.0: SP, due to a late power reduction at level off and an unanchored altimeter cross-check, did not preserve altitude within the specified limitation during cruise and turns. Deviation passed 300 feet and continued to diverge without being recognized. The IP took the controls to recover the assigned altitude and re-establish the formation in the assigned block.
texts.1: SP, due to an interrupted altimeter cross-check while re-establishing the visual reference on the other aircraft, allowed altitude to reach the 300 foot limit. The correction was started only after a verbal prompt from the IP and the return to the assigned altitude was slow. Altitude was regained, but the excursion was neither self-detected nor trapped in time.
texts.2: SP, due to a slightly late pitch correction after level off, let altitude drift between 150 and 300 feet from the assigned value. SP detected the trend on the altimeter without prompting and returned to the assigned altitude with a smooth and positive input. No intervention by the IP was required.
texts.3: SP maintained altitude within 150 feet during climb, level off, cruise and turns, applying pitch and power corrections early and smoothly. The altimeter was cross-checked at regular intervals without losing the visual reference on the formation.
texts.4: SP held altitude with deviations that remained negligible in every phase of flight, including turns and configuration changes. Corrections were anticipatory rather than reactive, so no excursion toward the tolerance ever developed.
texts.marginal: SP kept altitude within standards, but corrections were consistently applied only after the deviation had reached about two thirds of the allowable band, with a repeated tendency to descend in turns. The performance is acceptable while very little margin is left on this axis. SP is expected to anchor the altimeter earlier in the cross-check so that corrections begin at the first trend.

error_modes.label: Airspeed and energy control in formation

texts.0: SP, due to coarse and untimely throttle handling during climb and descent, did not preserve airspeed within the specified limitation. Deviation exceeded 20 knots and produced overshoots on both sides of the briefed value, with a closure rate the formation could not absorb. The IP intervened on the throttle to re-establish the briefed airspeed.
texts.1: SP, due to chasing the other aircraft with large throttle inputs instead of setting a known power value, allowed airspeed to reach the 20 knot limit. Airspeed was restored only after the IP called the deviation, and the correction itself overshot before settling. The energy state was recovered late.
texts.2: SP, due to a delayed power addition at the start of the climb, allowed airspeed to fall between 10 and 20 knots below the briefed value. SP recognized the decay on the airspeed indicator and restored the target with a smooth power correction. Recovery was made in time and without any input from the IP.
texts.3: SP maintained airspeed within 10 knots in all phases of flight, using small anticipatory power changes at level off and at each configuration change. The energy state remained predictable for the other aircraft in the formation throughout.
texts.4: SP flew airspeed with deviations that remained negligible, setting power ahead of each transition rather than correcting after it. Closure and separation stayed stable because the energy state was never allowed to drift.
texts.marginal: SP held airspeed inside standards, but a repeated tendency to arrive fast at level off required a visible power reduction each time. The deviations stayed short of the limit while the pattern was consistent across the sortie. SP is expected to set the level off power earlier so that airspeed stabilizes without a late correction.

error_modes.label: Exit heading on roll out from turns

texts.0: SP, due to an imprecise roll out reference and no use of the heading indicator during the recovery from the turn, did not roll out on the briefed heading. The exit heading error exceeded 10 degrees and the formation was left pointing away from the intended line. The IP directed and then flew the correction back to the assigned heading.
texts.1: SP, due to starting the roll out at the target heading instead of leading it, exited turns with a heading error at the 10 degree limit. The heading was corrected only after a verbal reminder and the subsequent correction turn was itself late. The briefed ground track was regained with delay.
texts.2: SP, due to a slightly late roll out from a turn flown at high bank, exited between 5 and 10 degrees off the briefed heading. SP identified the error immediately on the heading indicator and corrected with a smooth turn back to the assigned value. No prompting or intervention was needed.
texts.3: SP rolled out of turns within 5 degrees of the briefed exit heading, leading the roll out in proportion to the bank used. Heading control remained consistent both for turns flown as Leader and for repositioning as Wingman.
texts.4: SP exited every turn with a heading error that remained negligible, adjusting the lead point for the bank angle flown without any correction afterwards. The formation ground track matched the briefed profile throughout.
texts.marginal: SP kept exit headings within standards, but consistently rolled out on the outside of the target and then closed the last few degrees with a second correction. The final values were acceptable while the technique was not yet repeatable. SP is expected to lead the roll out so that the heading is captured in one movement.

error_modes.label: Prompt trim through configuration and power changes

texts.0: SP, due to flying against sustained out of trim control forces instead of trimming after each configuration and power change, did not trim the aircraft promptly throughout the flight phases. The residual stick force drove continuous pitch excursions beyond the allowed band and control inputs became coarse. The IP had to take the controls and re-trim the aircraft.
texts.1: SP, due to omitting trim after the power changes at level off, held the aircraft with constant control pressure. Trim was applied only after the IP pointed out the control force, by which time altitude and airspeed had drifted to the edge of the allowed band. Aircraft control became smooth only after that late trim input.
texts.2: SP, due to trimming in one late step instead of continuously, flew short periods with residual control force after level off. The resulting deviations stayed inside the allowed band and SP re-trimmed on own initiative once the state was recognized. Formation position was maintained without intervention.
texts.3: SP trimmed the aircraft promptly after each power, configuration and airspeed change, so control forces stayed neutral in all phases of flight. Formation position corrections were therefore made with small and precise inputs.
texts.4: SP kept the aircraft in trim continuously, anticipating the trim change that each configuration or power change would produce. Control forces were never allowed to build and station keeping remained stable with minimal effort.
texts.marginal: SP trimmed the aircraft within acceptable limits, but the trim was applied after the deviation appeared rather than with the change that caused it. The performance meets the standard while control inputs remain larger than necessary. SP is expected to trim as an integral part of every configuration and power change.

error_modes.label: G load control and formation energy awareness

texts.0: SP, due to abrupt aft stick during rejoins and turn reversals, did not maintain control of G load and formation energy as required. G exceeded the 4 G maximum set for the sortie and the energy state was left unusable for the following maneuver. The IP intervened on the controls to unload the aircraft.
texts.1: SP, due to correcting an overshoot with a single large pull instead of a controlled combination of bank and G, reached the 4 G maximum for the profile. The loading was reduced only after the IP called it and the aircraft was left low on energy afterwards. Control was regained, but not through SP's own recognition.
texts.2: SP, due to a slightly aggressive pull entering a turn, allowed G to rise well above the value the maneuver required while remaining below the sortie maximum. SP recognized the loading on the accelerometer and in the airspeed decay, then unloaded and re-established the turn smoothly. No intervention was required.
texts.3: SP monitored G throughout the sortie and kept the loading smooth and positive, well inside the 4 G maximum. Formation energy was preserved so that airspeed and altitude remained available for the next maneuver.
texts.4: SP managed G and formation energy so precisely that airspeed decay in turns matched exactly what the profile required, with no unloading correction needed at any point. The aircraft was never loaded beyond the demand of the maneuver.
texts.marginal: SP kept G within the sortie maximum, but loading was applied in steps rather than progressively and airspeed bled more than the maneuver required. The result is acceptable while the technique costs energy. SP is expected to blend bank and G so that the formation energy state is preserved.

error_modes.label: Leader smoothness and bank limits for the Wingman's position

texts.0: SP as Leader, due to rolling into turns at a rate and bank the Wingman could not match from the position flown, did not execute the maneuvers in a smooth manner. Bank exceeded the value allowed for that position, including bank beyond 60 degrees with the Wingman in Route, and the Wingman was driven outside his aircraft limitations. The IP assumed the Leader duties to restore a workable formation geometry.
texts.1: SP as Leader, due to selecting bank for the maneuver rather than for the position the Wingman was flying, used bank at the limit allowed for that position and reversed it abruptly. The roll rate was eased only after the IP prompted and the Wingman regained position with delay. The formation was held together by the Wingman's correction rather than by the Leader's technique.
texts.2: SP as Leader, due to a slightly rapid roll entry, briefly made station keeping harder for the Wingman during a turn flown at high bank. SP recognized the effect on the Wingman's position and moderated the roll rate and the bank without prompting. The Wingman regained a stable position and the maneuver continued as briefed.
texts.3: SP as Leader executed the maneuvers smoothly and kept bank within the value allowed for the Wingman's position, up to 90 degrees in Fingertip, 60 degrees in Route, 45 to 60 degrees in Echelon and 30 degrees for Crossunders. Roll rates and G onset were selected so that the Wingman was never driven toward his aircraft limitations.
texts.4: SP as Leader flew every maneuver so smoothly that the Wingman held position with minimal correction throughout, with bank and roll rate matched to the position flown at all times. Attention to the Wingman was continuous and visible in the choice of every input.
texts.marginal: SP as Leader stayed within the allowed bank for each position, but roll entries and reversals were sharp enough that the Wingman needed a visible correction each time. The maneuvers meet the standard while the smoothness required of the Leader is not yet consistent. SP is expected to moderate roll rate and G onset with the Wingman's position in mind.

error_modes.label: Radio calls and visual signals before maneuvers and configuration changes

texts.0: SP as Leader, due to failure to pass a required call at the briefed point, started maneuvers and changed the aircraft configuration without any radio call or visual signal to the Wingman. The Wingman was left to react to the Leader's aircraft instead of to a directive, and both position and separation degraded. The IP made the calls and directed the formation back to a safe geometry.
texts.1: SP as Leader, due to an indirect hint instead of a direct statement of the intended maneuver, gave calls that were incomplete or issued as the maneuver had already begun. The Wingman acted only after the IP clarified on the radio, and the configuration change was made with the Wingman still repositioning. The requirement was met in wording but not in timing.
texts.2: SP as Leader, due to a call passed later than briefed, signalled a turn with less warning than the Wingman needed. SP recognized the omission, repeated the call correctly and delayed the maneuver until the Wingman acknowledged. The remaining maneuvers and configuration changes were called on time and without prompting.
texts.3: SP as Leader gave the appropriate radio calls or visual signals to the Wingman before every maneuver, comm-out tactical turn and change of aircraft configuration. Calls were standard, timed to give the Wingman useful warning, and acknowledged before the maneuver began.
texts.4: SP as Leader passed every call and visual signal so precisely that the Wingman's actions were anticipatory throughout the sortie. Configuration changes and turns were transmitted with clear phraseology and never required repetition.
texts.marginal: SP as Leader passed all the required calls and signals, but several arrived close to the start of the maneuver, leaving the Wingman little time to prepare. The requirement is met while the margin given to the Wingman is thin. SP is expected to move the calls earlier so that the Wingman can set up before the maneuver begins.

error_modes.label: Checklist execution and informing the Wingman

texts.0: SP as Leader, due to running the checks from memory while attention stayed on the formation geometry, did not execute all checks according to the check list and did not inform the Wingman. Required items were omitted and the formation continued into the next phase in the wrong configuration. The IP had to stop the sequence and complete the checks.
texts.1: SP as Leader, due to an interrupted checklist flow on arrival in the working area, completed the checks late and informed the Wingman only after the IP prompted. The formation was already established in the profile before the check was called. Nothing was ultimately omitted, but the sequence was driven by the IP.
texts.2: SP as Leader, due to a slightly late start of the check, ran the check list after the point briefed for it. SP noticed the delay, completed every item from the check list and passed the required call to the Wingman without prompting. The profile then continued as briefed.
texts.3: SP as Leader executed all checks according to the check list at the briefed points and informed the Wingman on completion each time. Checklist discipline did not degrade lookout or formation control.
texts.4: SP as Leader integrated the check list into the flight so completely that every check was executed at the correct point, called to the Wingman and confirmed, with no effect on aircraft control. The timing left the formation fully prepared for each phase.
texts.marginal: SP as Leader completed all checks and passed the required information, but the checks were run as a hurried block that briefly reduced attention to the Wingman. The standard is met while the workload distribution is not. SP is expected to spread the check list across the available time so that lookout is preserved.

error_modes.label: Area boundaries and orientation as Leader

texts.0: SP as Leader, due to lack of awareness of the aircraft's position relative to the area boundary, did not keep the formation within the assigned area. The formation crossed the boundary and SP was unable to state a position or a heading back to mother base. The IP took over the navigation and returned the formation to the assigned area.
texts.1: SP as Leader, due to an orientation built on a single ground feature instead of continuous position keeping, allowed the formation to reach the edge of the assigned area. The turn back was made only after the IP pointed out the boundary and SP needed assistance to confirm the direction to mother base. The formation stayed inside the area, but not through SP's own monitoring.
texts.2: SP as Leader, due to a turn continued slightly past the briefed reversal point, closed on the area boundary during the working phase. SP recognized the position against the area limits and reversed the formation back toward the centre of the area in time. Orientation to mother base and to the alternate airport was retained throughout.
texts.3: SP as Leader knew the area borders, kept the formation well inside the assigned area and maintained orientation at all times, remaining able to return to mother base or the alternate airport on request. Position was checked against area references without any loss of formation control.
texts.4: SP as Leader managed the working area so that reversals were planned long before the boundary was approached, and could state position, heading home and alternate at any moment. Fuel, weather conditions and the flight area were exploited efficiently and the formation was kept fluid with minimal assistance from the IP.
texts.marginal: SP as Leader kept the formation inside the assigned area, but reversals were initiated close to the boundary and orientation was reconstructed rather than continuously held. The performance is within standards with little geographic margin. SP is expected to plan the reversal points earlier and to maintain a running position picture.

error_modes.label: Wingman reporting of limits and abnormal situations

texts.0: SP as Wingman, due to lack of assertiveness in voicing a recognized unsafe condition, did not report to the Leader when flight parameters reached their limits. The abnormal condition was allowed to persist while SP continued to fly position, and the formation was committed further into the profile. The IP made the call and directed the recovery.
texts.1: SP as Wingman, due to reluctance to interrupt the Leader's sequence, reported the parameter reaching its limit only after the IP prompted. The report was phrased in vague terms rather than stating the actual aircraft state, and the Leader adjusted the profile late. The condition was resolved, but the initiative came from the rear cockpit.
texts.2: SP as Wingman, due to a short delay while confirming the indication, reported the parameter to the Leader later than the situation allowed. SP then transmitted a clear and specific report without prompting and the Leader adjusted the maneuver in time. Aircraft control and G monitoring were maintained throughout.
texts.3: SP as Wingman maintained aircraft control, monitored G and reported to the Leader immediately whenever a flight parameter reached a limit or any abnormal situation was perceived. The reports were specific, timely and did not degrade station keeping.
texts.4: SP as Wingman monitored the aircraft state so closely that every approaching limit was reported before it was reached, in plain and unambiguous terms, while position and G control remained precise. The Leader was never required to ask for the information.
texts.marginal: SP as Wingman made all the required reports, but each followed a period of self-checking before transmitting, so the Leader received the information later than ideal. The reports were accurate and the standard is met. SP is expected to report the state as soon as it is recognized rather than after independent confirmation.
